title: How Money Laundering Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain money laundering: why drug traffickers and others need to wash dirty cash (especially US dollars), the three stages of placement, layering, and integration, and the tools used. Covered: the ten-thousand-dollar reporting threshold, the black market Colombian peso exchange, smurfing (structuring deposits), offshore secrecy jurisdictions and underground banking such as hawala and fei chien, shell versus front companies, and economic harms. Case examples include Crazy Eddie's Eddie Antar, economist Franklin Gerardo who laundered for Colombian kingpin Jose Santa Cruz Londono, and the DEA's Operation Juno sting in Atlanta. The episode ends with a plug for the Stuff You Should Know super-stuff economics audiobook, blog mentions, and an epilepsy and deja vu listener mail from Meg.

segments.title: Opening banter and Scarface
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about rainy Mondays, Karen Carpenter, and the movie Scarface, then introduce money laundering as the topic.

segments.title: Why launder money and the scale of the problem
segments.summary: Cash-heavy drug dealers need to wash dirty money because they cannot account for it. A million dollars in cash weighs about 256 pounds. Estimates put global laundering at $500 billion to $1 trillion a year, far more than the roughly $3 billion drug trade. US dollars are the main currency laundered because of US banking transparency laws.

segments.title: Placement, layering, and integration
segments.summary: The three stages of money laundering. Placement puts dirty cash into banks, which is riskiest because of the $10,000 reporting threshold. Layering spreads the money through transfers and purchases such as yachts. Integration returns the money to the legitimate economy.

segments.title: Enforcement agencies and offshore banking secrecy
segments.summary: US agencies such as the DOJ, FBI, IRS, and DEA hunt launderers, and the FATF and UN are involved globally. Secrecy jurisdictions such as Bahrain, the Caymans, Hong Kong, and Macau offer anonymous banking. Underground systems such as hawala and fei chien leave no paper trail.

segments.title: Black market Colombian peso exchange and smurfing
segments.summary: The black market Colombian peso exchange converts dirty US dollars into clean pesos by using them to buy American goods for Colombian importers. Smurfing, or structuring, breaks cash into deposits below $10,000 made by people called smurfs.

segments.title: Shell companies, front companies, and economic harm
segments.summary: Shell companies exist only on paper. Front companies are real businesses used to launder. Front companies can undercut honest businesses, and laundering can destabilize small economies and shift the tax burden onto ordinary taxpayers.

segments.title: Famous cases: Crazy Eddie, Franklin Gerardo, Operation Juno
segments.summary: Crazy Eddie's Eddie Antar skimmed millions to hide income from the IRS and was extradited from Israel. Economist Franklin Gerardo laundered about $36 million for Jose Santa Cruz Londono through banks in Europe and was caught after a neighbor's noise complaint. Operation Juno was a DEA sting in Atlanta that busted about 40 people and seized about 3,600 kilograms of cocaine.

segments.title: Super Stuff audiobook plug and blog shout-out
segments.summary: The hosts promote their Stuff You Should Know economics audiobook and their blog, and mention a how stuff works article on money laundering.

segments.title: Listener mail from Meg on epilepsy and deja vu
segments.summary: Meg, who has temporal lobe epilepsy, writes to say deja vu can be a simple partial seizure and that lavender smell and tunnel vision are also possible seizure symptoms.
